ai.definition: Tidal stream energy is a form of renewable energy that harnesses the kinetic energy from ocean tides using underwater turbines.
ai.howItWorks: Underwater turbines are placed in tidal streams where they rotate as water flows past them. The rotation generates electricity through conventional means, such as connecting to a generator. Turbines can be mounted on the seabed or float with the currents while still capturing energy from both ebb and flood tides.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the intermittency issues faced by wind and solar power, providing a more reliable source of electricity due to the predictable nature of tidal flows.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves designing, testing, and producing turbine components. Materials such as steel, composites, and electronics are used in the construction process.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes site selection, installation of turbines, connection to the grid, and commissioning. Turbines must be robust enough to withstand harsh marine environments.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include initial capital investment for turbine manufacturing and deployment, maintenance costs, and environmental impact assessments. Installation in deeper waters can increase costs significantly.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to grow as more projects are commissioned and technological advancements reduce costs and improve efficiency.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by country but generally involve environmental impact assessments, permitting processes, and adherence to maritime safety standards. Some regions offer incentives for renewable energy development.
ai.risks: Environmental risks include potential impacts on marine life and ecosystems. Technical challenges include corrosion in harsh environments and the need for robust design against extreme weather conditions.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable and depends on local market conditions, government incentives, and operational efficiency. Early projects may face higher costs but could become more profitable as technology improves and scales up.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development focuses on improving turbine designs to capture more energy efficiently, reducing installation and maintenance costs, and expanding into deeper waters where tidal currents are stronger.

glossary.def: A current of water caused by the rise and fall of tides in coastal areas.
The energy possessed by an object due to its motion.
A device designed to capture kinetic energy from flowing water and convert it into electrical power.

subsystems.name: Rotor
subsystems.role: Captures the kinetic energy of tidal currents; designed to work in both flood and ebb directions.

subsystems.name: Support structure
subsystems.role: Holds the turbine in the tidal stream, either on the seabed or floating.
parts: floating platform and moorings (for deep water)

subsystems.name: Electrical system
subsystems.role: Collects power and transmits it to shore.

subsystems.name: Control and monitoring
subsystems.role: Optimises power capture and protects the machine.

subsystems.name: Installation and maintenance equipment
subsystems.role: Enables deployment and servicing in strong currents.

buildSteps.title: Survey the site
buildSteps.detail: Measure tidal current speeds, direction and seabed conditions over a full spring–neap cycle; assess environmental impact.

buildSteps.title: Design and model
buildSteps.detail: Use computational fluid dynamics and scale-model tank tests to optimise blade shape and array layout for the local tidal flow.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture turbine
buildSteps.detail: Fabricate blades from glass or carbon fibre composites; assemble nacelle with generator, gearbox and control systems.

buildSteps.title: Build foundation
buildSteps.detail: Weld a steel monopile or cast a concrete gravity base; for floating units, assemble the platform and mooring lines.

buildSteps.title: Install foundation
buildSteps.detail: Use a heavy-lift vessel to drive or position the foundation on the seabed, ensuring it can withstand tidal loads.

buildSteps.title: Install turbine
buildSteps.detail: Lift the nacelle and rotor onto the foundation, or tow out a fully assembled floating unit and connect its moorings.

buildSteps.title: Lay and connect cables
buildSteps.detail: Bury or protect subsea cables from turbine to shore; connect to the onshore grid substation.

buildSteps.title: Commission and test
buildSteps.detail: Run the turbine through its speed range, verify pitch control in both flow directions, and synchronise with the grid.

buildSteps.title: Operate and maintain
buildSteps.detail: Monitor performance remotely; schedule maintenance during slack tide windows with service vessels and ROVs.

prerequisites.why: Light, strong blades are needed to withstand salt water and cyclic loads.
They carry electricity from the seabed to shore reliably.
Installing and servicing turbines in strong tidal currents requires specialised vessels and remote tools.
Accurate prediction of tidal currents is essential for siting and grid planning.
Seawater corrodes steel and marine growth degrades performance; coatings and alloys are improving but not fully solved.
Coastal substations and cables must be available to accept the power.

pathway.milestone: Single turbines and small arrays (e.g. the MeyGen project in Scotland, a few megawatts)
pathway.unlocks: Proof of concept and early grid experience.

pathway.milestone: Multi-megawatt arrays of 10–50 MW with several turbines sharing infrastructure
pathway.unlocks: Economies of scale and lower cost per megawatt-hour.

pathway.milestone: Floating tidal stream platforms for deeper water
pathway.unlocks: Access to more sites and easier maintenance.

pathway.milestone: Hundreds-of-megawatt tidal farms integrated with offshore grid hubs
pathway.unlocks: Predictable, firm renewable power at utility scale.
